passage: Nursery note, Thursday. Abhinav, two, turned his whole head toward me each time I began the counting song, eyes bright, and edged closer on the mat. At lunch he took three spoonfuls of dal and rice, then turned his head away and held his lips together. I lowered the spoon and said, “All done?” He looked back at me and smiled. I put the bowl aside. He ate a banana later. 🙂 Yusuf

qa.q: How many spoonfuls did Abhinav take at lunch before turning away?
qa.a: Three spoonfuls of dal and rice.

qa.q: What might Abhinav's head turn away from the spoon mean, and what else could it be?
qa.a: He most likely felt full and content, wanting to stop, and his smile afterwards showed he was happy. It could also mean he wanted something different.

qa.q: Why was Yusuf's response helpful?
qa.a: Yusuf respected the turn-away, which shows Abhinav that his signals count, and still offered food later.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel when the spoon goes down?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and understood, and be more willing to eat again at the next meal.

grounding: A toddler turns toward a caregiver to engage and turns away to end feeding, and the caregiver respects the signal.

passage: On the mud verandah, Kiran hummed an old lullaby while she plaited her own hair. Her granddaughter Salma, two, who had been playing with pebbles, turned her head toward the sound and crawled over into her lap. Kiran held a cup of warm milk to her lips. Salma took two sips and then turned her face to the wall, lips closed. Kiran waited, then set the cup on the step. “Later, then,” she said, and went on humming.

qa.q: What did Salma turn her head toward on the verandah?
qa.a: The sound of Kiran humming an old lullaby.

qa.q: What could Salma's turn to the wall mean, and what else might it be?
qa.a: It probably means she was done with the milk. It could also mean she was too warm or wanted to keep listening to the song.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that helped?
qa.a: She waited, did not push the cup and kept humming, so Salma stayed close and comfortable.

qa.q: How might Salma feel when her signal is respected?
qa.a: She may feel that turning away is enough to be heard, which builds trust that she does not have to cry to be understood. 🙂

grounding: A toddler turns toward a caregiver to engage and away to end feeding, and the caregiver respects the turn-away.

passage:
In the small kitchen of their Seoul flat, Leila held out another spoon of rice porridge. Jin turned his head sharply away to the window.
"Here comes the plane!" She flew the spoon round. Jin turned further, lips tight.
Leila put the spoon down. "All done? Okay." She wiped his hands.
A moment later Jin turned back toward her, smiled and babbled, "Ba-ba-ba," reaching for her sleeve.

qa.q: What was Leila feeding Jin?
qa.a: Rice porridge.

qa.q: What did Jin's turn to the window mean, and how did he feel afterwards?
qa.a: It meant he was done eating and wanted the feed to end; once Leila stopped, he seemed content and friendly, turning back to babble.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: The plane game ignored his signal and made him turn further away; putting the spoon down and saying "All done" fixed it.

qa.q: How might Leila feel when Jin turns back and reaches for her sleeve?
qa.a: She would likely feel reassured and warm, seeing that stopping the feed didn't push him away.

grounding: A toddler turns his head away to end a feed and turns back toward the carer to engage once it is respected.

passage:
I'm Jatin, Gurleen's cousin. On Sunday I sang her the elephant song, and she turned right toward me, eyes shining. I sang it again. And again. The fourth time, she turned her head away to the wall and pulled at her ear. I kept singing louder.
"She's finished, Jatin," Masi said. "Let her be."
I stopped. After a bit, Gurleen turned back and poked my nose. I'm still not sure if she was bored or just tired.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do the fourth time Jatin sang?
qa.a: She turned her head away to the wall and pulled at her ear.

qa.q: What might Gurleen have been feeling when she turned away?
qa.a: She was probably bored or tired of the song and wanted a break; poking Jatin's nose later shows she still felt friendly toward Jatin.

qa.q: What could Jatin try next time Gurleen turns away?
qa.a: Stop singing and wait quietly, as Masi suggested, and let Gurleen choose when to turn back.

qa.q: How does Masi see Gurleen's turn to the wall?
qa.a: Masi reads it as a clear "finished" signal that should be respected, not ignored.

grounding: A cousin notices a toddler turning toward the singer to engage and away to end the game, and learns to respect it.

passage:
Monday: Harish turned his head away from the bottle. Darshan, his father, kept nudging it back to his lips. Harish arched, spluttered and cried.
Thursday: Harish turned away again. This time Darshan lifted the bottle away and waited. After a minute, Harish turned back and drank calmly.
The next Monday: when Darshan walked in from work, Harish turned toward him at once, grinning, both hands reaching.

qa.q: What happened on Monday when Darshan kept nudging the bottle?
qa.a: Harish arched, spluttered and cried.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when he turned away on Monday?
qa.a: He was likely full or needed a pause, and feeling pushed made him upset, which is why he arched and cried.

qa.q: What did Darshan change on Thursday, and why did it help?
qa.a: He took the bottle away and waited, so Harish's signal was respected and he could come back to drink calmly.

qa.q: What might Darshan feel when Harish turns toward him grinning?
qa.a: He would probably feel happy and close to his son, sensing that Harish trusts him. 😊

grounding: Over several days a father learns to respect his toddler's head turn away during feeds, and the child turns toward him to engage.

passage:
In the Guwahati flat, Hafsa sat on the floor with a bowl of khichdi. Bhupen turned his head towards her, mouth open, babbling between spoonfuls.
After a few more bites he turned his head away and stared at the window.
Hafsa held the spoon near his lips. He turned further.
“All done?” she asked, and put the bowl down. “Okay, finished.”
Bhupen swung his head back and grinned, then crawled off to his blocks.

qa.q: What was in Hafsa's bowl?
qa.a: The bowl had khichdi in it.

qa.q: What does Bhupen turning his head away suggest he wanted?
qa.a: It suggests he was full or had simply had enough and wanted the meal to end; he seemed content, not upset, once she stopped.

qa.q: Why was putting the bowl down a good choice?
qa.a: It showed Bhupen that his turn-away was heard, so he learns his signals matter and meals stay pleasant.

qa.q: What would change if Hafsa kept pushing the spoon?
qa.a: Bhupen might get frustrated and fuss, and learn that turning away does not work, making meals a struggle.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler turning his head towards a caregiver to engage and away to end a feed, and the caregiver respecting it.
